newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Balkan turmoil bubbles but Slovenia gets government.
newsitem.headline: Balkan turmoil bubbles but Slovenia gets government.

text.p: Political turmoil kept bubbling across the Balkans on Friday and savers ruined by get-rich-quich investment schemes torched a town hall in southern Albania.

The small Alpine state of Slovenia escaped from two months of post-election stalemate. Serbia's deadlocked rivals pulled back from a rare outbreak of violence over control of local news media in Kragujevac.
But Bulgaria, trapped in political paralysis and dire economic straits, seemed no closer to getting a new government
In the Albanian city of Lushnje, demonstrators set fire to the town hall and ransacked a cinema in protest at the loss of their savings.

"Thousands of people gathered in front of the town hall. The people were angry and out of control and they set fire to the town hall," the radio said. "They have started to destroy the cinema," the radio added.

Albania is Europe's poorest country and thousands of people were sold homes and livestock to pump money into pyramid investment houses which sprang up in the aftermath of communism with promises of instant wealth.
A series of bankruptcies has led to a rash of street demonstrations by angry savers who blame the rightwing government for failing to prevent their losses.

In Bulgaria, where political stalemate has blocked the formation of a new government to rescue a collapsing economy, about 2,000 students carried flaming torches through Sofia's evening fog to back opposition demands for a general election.

Despite a collapse of public support driven home by 18 days of opposition street protests, the ruling Socialists insist that control of parliament entitles them to name the new prime minister to replace Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.
Cracks have begun to appear in the Socialists' parliamentary majority but talks between the rival factions showed no sign of producing a compromise.
"It is clear that no dialogue is possible and we see no reason for further talks," opposition leader Ivan Kostov told the Sophia rally. "Victory will be ours."

Serbia's ruling Socialists struck a compromise with the opposition on Friday over control of local media in a provincial city hit by political violence rare in their 10-week dispute over local election results.

In Kragujevac, an industrial city of 200,000 south of Belgrade captured by the opposition November, the two rivals agreed that television, radio and the local newspaper would drop all political coverage and comment until the courts settle who should be in charge.
Some 200 police, who guarded the local broadcasting station, when it was surrounded by opposition protesters on Thursday, left the buildings after the deal was negotiated.
Riot police clubbed sit-in protesters aside to clear a highway into Kragujevac on Thursday, beating one member of parliament unconscious.

It was one of the few violent incidents in more than two months of demonstrations in which the opposition is trying to to force President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists to accept defeat in 14 cities.
The country-wide protests show no signs of ending.

"We have brought the ideals of democracy back to Serbia and become once more a people who believe in something," the opposition's Zoran Djindjic told 30,000 supporters at a Friday rally in central Belgrade.
In relatively prosperous Slovenia, a long post-election stalemate seemed over when Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek of the centre-left Liberal Democrats formed his new cabinet.

The general election of November 10 left parliament balanced between left and right. Drnovsek, who tried and failed to bring rightwing parties into a broad coalition, retains power thanks to a single member who defected from the other side.
